title: Tesla, SpaceX target 2028 Terafab chip production
html:
Tesla and SpaceX are targeting Terafab chip production at their planned semiconductor complex in Grimes County, Texas, during the third or fourth quarter of 2028. Elon Musk outlined the timetable during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call on 20 October 2026, saying that ASML and other semiconductor equipment suppliers were accelerating deliveries to support the project.

Musk acknowledged that the schedule was highly ambitious and subject to considerable uncertainty. The first milestone is a functioning test chip from the project’s research fabrication facility in Austin, Texas, expected in May or June 2027. The initial device will use static random-access memory (SRAM) structures to evaluate the manufacturing process before more complex processors enter production.

ASML deliveries and Terafab chip production

Access to advanced lithography equipment is one of the project’s most significant constraints. During the earnings call, an analyst asked whether SpaceX had placed orders for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems from ASML, the Dutch manufacturer that supplies the equipment used to produce leading-edge semiconductor devices.

Musk did not directly confirm the status of those orders or disclose equipment quantities and delivery dates. Instead, he thanked ASML and other suppliers for accelerating their deliveries. His comments indicate that equipment availability is being addressed, although ASML has not independently confirmed a revised delivery schedule for Terafab.

The scale of the challenge is considerable. EUV lithography machines are among the most complex items of semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and their production capacity is limited. ASML’s EUV systems are essential for manufacturing the smallest features in advanced logic and memory devices.

According to information reported by Reuters in September, ASML was already close to selling out its available EUV production capacity for 2027. The company was examining ways to manufacture more than 110 systems in 2028 to accommodate increasing demand.

Intel’s role in Terafab

Intel joined the Terafab initiative in April 2026, contributing semiconductor process development, fabrication and advanced packaging expertise. Musk subsequently indicated that the project would use Intel’s 14A process technology, although the precise commercial and technical arrangements have not been publicly detailed.

As previously reported by eeNews Europe in its examination of the Intel-Terafab partnership, the availability of leading-edge manufacturing equipment and the time needed to establish a stable fabrication process represent substantial obstacles to the project’s timetable.

SpaceX and Tesla originally announced Terafab in March 2026. In August, SpaceX identified Grimes County as the location of the main manufacturing complex, near Gibbons Creek Reservoir. The research facility at Tesla’s Austin campus is intended to support process development before manufacturing is scaled at the larger site.

The initial phase is estimated to require approximately $16.8 billion in capital investment. The proposed vertically integrated operation would combine logic and memory semiconductor manufacturing with advanced packaging and testing, producing devices for Tesla vehicles, Optimus robots and SpaceX’s proposed space-based computing infrastructure.

A compressed manufacturing timetable

Building and commissioning a leading-edge semiconductor fabrication facility ordinarily takes several years. The equipment must be installed, calibrated and qualified, while the manufacturing process must demonstrate acceptable yields before commercial production can begin.

Musk described the late-2028 target as an aspiration rather than a firm commitment. The broader Terafab programme has a long-term objective of producing enough computing hardware to deliver 1 TW of processing capacity annually, but the companies have not disclosed a detailed manufacturing ramp-up schedule.

Terafab chip production in 2028 therefore remains an internal target. Accelerated equipment deliveries could shorten part of the construction and commissioning process, but they do not eliminate the technical challenges associated with bringing an advanced semiconductor fabrication line into volume production.
